utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's a conclusion, and given my role, I don't know to what extent I may draw conclusions. But I told you about an event that happened which related to the search for someone whose last name was Markovic. I remember that fact because he was a forensic expert in the police force, and when we went to carry out on-site investigations, he was a fairly good professional and that is why we remembered him. That's what he was well known for. And that is one of the reasons for which I agreed to go there with these people, because in the hope that they would find something there, they wanted a judge to be present to make a record of everything. As to what went on in that school, to this very day it's a controversial issue for me because I have heard contradictory claims, claims that people were seriously abused in that school and claims that it was a traditional camp in the centre of the town and then there were also claims according to which nothing had happened there. I know that certain people from the music school were dealt with for what had happened in the music school, and I think that these were cases dealt with in some of the courts in Zenica. As to what is true, it's very difficult to say right now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And my last question: If you remember, you spoke about a meeting in Hotel Internacional. I'd like to know whether you could specify the date and say which -- who was the president of the court at the time. Was it your colleague Kovac or Colakovic who attended that meeting with you?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was Colakovic, but I'm not certain about the date. The year was perhaps 1993. I know it was immediately after the arrival of Mr. Hadzihasanovic. Various meetings were held, but I really don't remember the date. I know that I participated in that, and I warned them about the problems of vehicles and the school. That's why I remember attending that event. Then I remember the monitors in white. I know that there were two of them sitting at the table to the left. Mr. Hadzihasanovic was sitting on the opposite side of the table, two or three places away from me. I remember that on the basis of what I could observe. But as to the date, well, I might even be wrong as far as the year is concerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Adamovic. My colleague has something he would like to say. Just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those are all the questions that I wanted to ask you. Thank you for answering them. Mr. President, as far as the documents are concerned, the ones that we would like to tender into evidence, I think it would be best to proceed as we did last time. And if we don't have time today, we could inform you on Monday of the documents that we would like to tender into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That's how we will proceed. Does the other Defence team have any questions for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. During the pause, the Defence team for Mr. Kubura agreed that we had no questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Benjamin, before the Judges ask the witness some questions, are there any other questions you would like to put to this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution has no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Well, I will first start to put questions to the witness, and then the other two Judges will also ask the witness some questions. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, first of all, I would like you to clarify your current position. I think you said that you were a judge at the Supreme Court. Is that the court of annunciation or is it the constitutional court, and when were you appointed to this position?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name of the court is the Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the competence this court has, does it have ample competence?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was just waiting for the interpreters. I am trying to speak a little more slowly for the sake of the interpreters, but I could speak more rapidly. It has supreme competence in the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina as far as interpreting legal provisions are concerned. And to an extent, it has competence for first-level judgements for the most serious crimes, for terrorism, drugs, organised crime, et cetera. It also has an appellate section, and it has a special section for organised crime, and the Chamber members are also judges from foreign countries. We even have French, Portuguese, American, and German judges. Similarly, there is a special section formed for dealing with cases for which there are reasonable grounds that war crimes were committed. And that part of the section should be taking over some of the cases from this Tribunal. I am a member of that court and I've been a member of that court for a year and a half, and I'm working as a judge in a certain case. Yesterday I said that we contested two systems, and the judge is now controlling the investigation carried out by the prosecution. The name of this judge is the judge for the previous case, and the judge who confirms the indictment and listens to testimony and decides on objections is called the judge for preliminary processes. So I dealt with this for a year and a half on my own. But everything that has entered into the Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina from when it started operating until about 15 days ago, I dealt with these matters. I also dealt with the preliminary procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Could you tell me when you were appointed to this position in this court.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think when I was appointed it was January --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean --

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was January 2003. And as soon as I was appointed, I started dealing with these matters, after the first session when the judges were assigned. I must say that I have difficulty remembering dates but there is a written record of all of this. I think it was in January 2003.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday, in response to a question put to you by the Defence, we found out - and this is something that we didn't know - that the accused, before they were transferred to The Hague, were presented to you. Within what legal context did you act?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I was the judge of the Supreme Court of the Federation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the Supreme Court of the Federation had the competence to take measures that involved transferring accused?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite right. Because in this organisation in the state structure, you have the BH Federation, you have Republika Srpska. These are the two components. Each entity has its own Supreme Court. I was a member of the Federation Supreme Court, and the people who on the basis of indictments -- international indictments from the Tribunal were deprived of their freedom in the territory of the Federation were taken to the Supreme Court so that proceedings to deliver them to the Tribunal could be carried out. So at the time, I was a judge who had to deal with such cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll go back to the period of the year 1993. And we have a document in evidence, the document number is 419. According to this document, the judges who were members of the military court were Mr. Kovac, who was the president from the 1st of September, 1992 to the 14th of June, 1993. You yourself are mentioned as a judge from the 1st of September, 1992 until the 31st of July, 1996. Apparently Mr. Kovac was no longer the president from the 14th of June, 1993. Who replaced him?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Decisions were taken by the Presidency about these matters, and Mr. Muhamed Colakovic replaced him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was replaced by Mr. Muhamed Colakovic, who was a judge from the 1st of January, 1993. Mr. Colakovic replaced Mr. Kovac, then; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You yourself - and this is what we have understood from your answers - you were the investigating judge or the judge who was responsible for investigations, but you were also the president of a Chamber that had to put on trial individuals who were being prosecuted. Because the Defence has shown us judgements according to which you were the president of the Chamber, and we saw that Mr. Kovac was the predecessor. Would you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, in that court, I did everything that a judge could do, because circumstances were such that I had a lot of experience in the judicial system from before and I was familiar with all the proceedings. I had already participated in all the stages of proceedings. So it was very easy for me to do any sort of work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And why weren't you appointed as the president to replace Mr. Kovac?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when we first discussed about establishing the court, a document was sent to Sarajevo according to which I would be the president of the court. But when we received a document -- a document was returned and the decision was not such. At the time, they stated that my name was the wrong kind of name for that area, given my nationality. That's what my colleague said and people close to me. I assume that that was the case in 1993. So there was a certain amount of suspicion, a lack of trust.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To clarify something, you mentioned your ethnic -- the ethnic group you belong to. What is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am a Croat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In response to numerous and varied questions put to you by the Defence, you said that you were an independent judge, but that's obvious if one is a judge. But the Trial Chamber would like to know who was above you in reality. Which ministry was above you? And you received a salary. But who paid you?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first -- I really need to explain this. At first there was a lot of ignorance in terms of the organisation. The former officers of the JNA were used to having military courts within the military system, and they advocated the situation in which the military would be totally separated and have their own courts. There was a meeting in Zenica attended by the late President Izetbegovic that I have already mentioned, and I happened to be there at the time. And in Zenica the initial conversations and negotiations about the establishment of those courts started. It was a very informal meeting at which it was decided that the military courts should use civilian laws, that they shouldn't be part of the military structures, and this all would serve to protect human rights and uphold conventions; that we should not mix court-martials with regular courts, that we should not allow commanders to manipulate with formal authorities [as interpreted]; that we should not allow people who lacked skills and education to try cases. It was wartime and the inner circle of people know that. President Izetbegovic said, "Okay, whatever has been said, why don't you put it on paper." And I do have that paper that was sent through unofficial channels to Sarajevo, all that has been said so far. And later on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your superior ministry was the Ministry of Defence, the Ministry of Justice, or the President of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Who signed your salary slips, that is?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first, because of the lack of organisation, there was nothing on my salary payslip because we did not receive any salaries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But once you did start receiving salaries, who signed your payslip?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the Ministry of Defence at first and later on the Ministry of Justice, and so on and so forth. And these things changed within the state structure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the Ministry of Defence was paying your salary until then?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the Prosecutor mentioned that yesterday. I don't know. In any case, we wanted to be part of the Ministry of Justice, that irrespective of the fact that we were called military courts we wanted to be a part of the civilian structure. It was wartime. Information circulated very slowly, and as the state was being organised, this was shifted from one ministry to another. At the end of the day it was decided that anybody who could pay us should pay us, as long as they could provide us for us and allow us to exist as a court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The administrative personnel, the Registry, the secretary of the court, were they civilians, were they people delegated by the Ministry of Defence? And who was paying their salaries, the administrative staff of the court?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire court was paid in the same way. And the personnel that was employed was the personnel of the civilian courts, where there was less work at the time, and they were well versed with the job. In any case, one has to understand that we were established by the Presidency, that our ultimate responsibility was towards the Presidency, and in the carriage of justice we were responsible to the appellate courts. The Presidency issued all sorts of decisions to assign us to various ministries, depending on the available resources or the current organisation of the administration of the state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we, then, conclude that since there were administrative problems, and whenever there are administrative problems, lack of personnel, telephone lines were not working, there was no paper, the president of the court would turn to the Presidency rather than to various ministers, the Minister of Defence or the Minister of Justice or what have you?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That would have been a logical thing to do. However, it was impossible to directly communicate to the Presidency, so we had to turn to various ministries to resolve the matter at hand. Sometimes it would be the Minister of Defence, sometimes it would be the Minister of Justice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your response, you said that you were situated in a building where there was also a civilian court, and you also told us that the prosecutor's office was in the same building on a lower floor and that you were above them. The civilian prosecutor's office was in the same building, on the same floor as the military prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The building where we were situated was the former building of the so-called Court of the Associated Labour. It was a very specific court which dealt with all the cases stemming from work relations and employment. That court stopped functioning, and since the building belonged to the state, we were located in that building. And from the moment we entered the building, that is, the military institutions, civilian institutions were no longer there. On the first floor was the prosecutor's office, and on the second floor was the court and the courtrooms. The civilian district court was in a different building. On the first floor of that building was the district court, and on the second floor was the civilian prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your building, where you had your offices on the second floor and the prosecutor's office was on the first floor, in that building was there a place or a sign on which one could read that these offices belonged to the prosecutor's office? And was there a soldier on duty who was on guard in front of those offices?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Whatever you have just said is correct. There was a flag which was put up according to law. There was an inscription. There was a sign in two languages, in two scripts, saying that this was a district military court. And the whole building was guarded by the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you climbed to your floor, you must have come across the prosecutor. Or when he wanted to see you, he would climb to your floor? How did that -- how was that organised?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the long winter afternoon when there was no heating, we would all meet in one room which was heated to a certain extent, and that's how we managed to survive. And at those moments we'd forget who the prosecutor was and who the judge was. We left that for the courtroom situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So when you found yourselves in that room where you came for heating, did you discuss your job? Did you exchange information and experiences and ideas? Did you talk about the problems? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was always the case and there was always an opportunity to discuss all that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to come back to that when I come back to the issue of the dead bodies. I have another topic that I would like to discuss with you, and that is the duration of detention. You have already replied to similar questions, but can you be more precise and tell us what was the law on a civilian person who was detained or kept in custody. What was the status of such a person? Was the military in a position to guard a civilian who was in custody and for how long before the judiciary, either the civilian or the military, were informed about that? So what would be the answer to this very precise question? I would like to know: A civilian who was arrested, for how long the police could keep that person in custody.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are talking hours here. 24 hours, 48 hours, or 72 hours. Not more than three days, in any case. I'm talking about the prosecutor, the police, and the judge altogether could keep that person for no longer than three days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A civilian, according what you have told us, who was arrested could be kept for a maximum of 1993 days, and then he had to be turned over to the judge, who was a civilian judge or military judge? Are you saying yes?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if a person after three days was not turned to the judge, what was the situation, the legal situation of that person who was not turned to a judge?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that person was in custody, then his status was illegal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A civilian judge or a military judge, with regard to the personal or public freedom, did he have a role to play? And if a judge would learn that a person was illegally kept in custody, what would a judge do in 1993?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A judge could not do anything. It was the prosecutor who could have instigated proceedings against that person who kept somebody in custody illegally, save for one situation: If the persons were detained or kept in custody, the president of the court or the investigating judge could make rounds of the detention unit in order to control the conditions of the detention. And if they came across a person who was illegally detained, then they could issue an order for this person to be immediately released, and this was the only case when this was possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as the person -- place which was considered an official detention unit in Zenica, was there an official prison in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a civilian detention unit and one part of that civilian detention unit was used by the military court for the detention of the military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In lieu of the civilian police that belonged to the MUP, was there a place where the military police could detain persons for up to three days?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To your knowledge, the military police, which was attached to the 3rd Corps, could they be controlled by the military prosecutor with regard to the detention of prisoners before the judge could intervene?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The prosecutor and the judge knew that this place was official detention unit, just like you can tell me now that this is the official courtroom of the Tribunal. And if I come to you convinced of that fact, I will go away from here in the belief that you only had one official courtroom. But you, on the other hand, may be using other rooms that you never showed to me. The prosecutor and the judge went by what was said to them, that those were officially the detention units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The building where you worked, well, how far was it from the music school? What was the distance between the two buildings?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday 150 to 300 metres. One building could be seen from the other. There is just one square, the central city square, between these two buildings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. As you were walking to your workplace, did you have to pass by the music school or in front of it?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was the music school guarded by anybody, or could anybody walk into it easily?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were always guards in front of the music school, and the citizens did not like that school, and even if somebody had shown inclination to enter it, they would not want to enter it because of all the rumours and stories.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that there were rumours about the music school. What rumours were those and stories?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you that the whole city was rife with rumours about the music school, the music school being a detention camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are saying that there were rumours about the music school being a detention unit. When you were drinking coffee with the prosecutor, did you talk about that issue?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On several occasions -- and it was not always the same person, because the chief prosecutor was not always the same -- on several occasions the judges would ask the prosecutor whether they had ever dealt with the issue of this music school, and the answer would be that something was being done or something had been done, but I know that there were cases pending before the court at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They would say, "We're working on it," but they didn't do anything, as a matter of fact; is that true?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether anything was done or not, I don't know. But the answer was always, "Something is being done. We're working on it."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you ever receive information from the families of the alleged detainee that their relatives were detained in the music school when you were acting as a judge? Did you ever receive such information?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both in my private capacity as well as in my professional capacity I received this information, and now I'm saying "in my private capacity"; why am I saying that? I didn't want to answer that, but you asked me, and it was my ethnic background that put me in that position. Very few people of other ethnic backgrounds were in high positions, when we are talking about this segment of life. So Croats would come to me. They would either come to the president of the local political party or to the local priest or to myself, and they would come to us because of our ethnic background. I have to say that publicly: because they believed they could easily convey information to us and that they would receive some sort of answer. I remember having asked an elderly gentleman why he didn't go to the police, and he told me, "Well, they will never believe me, because I'm not a Bosniak." Obviously, again we are talking rumours and stories. What the truth of the matter was, I wouldn't be able to tell you. However, the truth of the matter is that people did come to me. And when that happened in the court or even outside, when they would come across me somewhere on the street -- the prosecutor heard all this information, and not only the prosecutor. You see, from the way I worked, I alerted everybody. I could alert the army and the civilian prosecutor and everybody else. And the local priest did the same. The head of the local Croatian party also did the same, because those were the people that the Croats addressed most about those things. This was another result of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovac, the tribunal's president, the court's president, or the person who replaced him, usually when one is the president of a court one encounters the civilian authorities, the political authorities and the military authorities. Did the president of the court meet the 3rd Corps commander? As far as you know, did such a meeting ever take place?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to make a distinction between these two persons. I didn't have any successful cooperation with President Kovac and I said so openly on a number of occasions, because he wasn't a criminal judge. That wasn't his vocation. He wasn't familiar with the basics of such work. And I believe that he led the court in an erroneous manner, gave it too much official authority, because he didn't have any knowledge of the proceedings. Mr. Colakovic is a different kettle of fish. He's a professional criminal judge, and as opposed to President Kovac, he didn't take any decisions on his own without us knowing where the president was going, who he had contact with, et cetera, et cetera, because this other person did everything on his own, on an independent basis, and we knew nothing about this. President Colakovic was a gentleman, so to speak. He assembled the judges. We discussed what we should do, and he implemented these things. He was, so to speak, in the real sense of the term, primus inter pares, first among equals, and he knew that we had contact with the civilian and military organs, and once these organs decided to organise various kinds of meet, he would have contact with them, and on other occasions he would have contact with them when he wanted to discuss a court problem and wanted to resolve the problem. And this can be seen from the written documents. And there are far more such documents from the period when Mr. Colakovic was in charge of the court. At the time, I was his deputy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But did he meet the 3rd Corps commander? Did he see him, and was he able to inform him of the concerns that you and your colleagues had?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were such occasions when court presidents would meet corps commanders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you don't know what was said.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was there as the deputy of the president, well, then I know what was said. But as for the more frequent meetings that I didn't attend, I don't know what was said. But President Colakovic would inform all the judges. He would tell them that something would be dealt with for the court, that we'd receive documents, humanitarian parcels, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As the court was a military one, were there any lawyers there to defend the accused? And how many lawyers were there in the local bar?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, not many. I don't think there were more than 50 active lawyers at the time. But whenever the law stated that the accused or a suspect should have Defence counsel, we contacted counsel. From the judgements you saw, you can see how seriously this was approached, because it's fair to say that not a single judgement from 1993 is different from judgements from 1989 or 1999. The approach was completely professional. Naturally, there were experienced judges, capable judges. If you find any errors, then these were errors committed by young judges, judges who didn't have much experience and given the war they happened to be there. The senior judges worked very professionally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that you belonged to an ethnic group of Croats. Were there lawyers who also belonged to the Croat ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were lawyers of all nationalities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as you know, the families of those who were detained must have had access to lawyers. I assume that was the case.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as you know, did these lawyers try to take the people responsible in the military to task?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were such activities. I know this from the records. If we're talking about lawyers and nationalities, this all comes down to the personality of the person concerned. A normal person would do his job. But if the person wasn't a normal person - not crazy but just not normal - then he would emphasise a person part of his life, because that was what was important at the time. In my opinion, the most successful lawyer when defending someone of another nationality was perhaps a lawyer who was a Bosniak, a professional who did his job and wasn't interested in the nationality of a given person. He just did what he had to do; he did his job. Nationality was a subject that was manipulated very often in the course of the war. People were protected for these reasons, were promoted for these reasons. There was suspicion for these reasons. And this wasn't dangerous when it concerned people who didn't have any official authority. But when people in authority acted this way, then it's completely senseless. The fact that President Colakovic was a good man is that he appointed me as the deputy president in the court. He didn't have to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will now deal with a far more legal issue, which concerns the prosecutor referring a case to the judges. The Defence tried to get some explanations about this from you, and I must say that I'm not quite clear about this matter yet. I would like to know -- you'll see my question is very precise: When the Prosecution files a motion for a judge to deal with a violation -- we've been shown a number of documents and we can see that the prosecutor makes a request and it's his obligation to provide a legal description of the act that could be considered to be a violation. Once this document has been drafted, we understand that an investigating judge is designated and he carries out his work and then the trial starts. So my question is as follows: At the last stage, at the trial stage, do the judges have the power to change the description of the act concerned? Let's take an example. Let's take an act described as a simple theft by the prosecutor and the judge believes that in fact it's more than just a theft; it might be described as a crime or even as a war crime. In such a case, is it possible for the judge to provide an exact legal description of the act if the judge sees the affair in rem? What could you tell me about this? The Defence tried to obtain a response. I don't think they did. I would like to know whether you, who were involved in judging cases, had the possibility of saying that the events that were described in a certain manner were in fact events or acts that should be described in a different manner. Were you in a position, did you have the possibility of changing the legal description of the act concerned? As you can see, the question is very precise, and the answer should be either yes or no.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In answer, well, there is not a single lawyer who could answer just yes or no without this being ambiguous. The answer is yes, but that's not quite correct. Why? Because the judges had the right to change the legal qualification of an act, because the traditional accusatory principle would be applied. A trial would be initiated as the request of the prosecutor. The judge wasn't bound or isn't bound by the legal qualification. If the legal qualification is murder, this is something the judges are informed of. The judge is bound by the factual description, by the objective description that has to do with person against whom an indictment has been issued. So we're talking about the subject of an objective element with regard to the description of the event and the factual description of the event mentioned in the indictments. We could say, "No, this is a crime but it is not the crime of murder. It is the crime of serious bodily harm, inflicting serious bodily harm which resulted in death." So the perpetrator didn't intend to kill the person but intended to inflict serious bodily harm; but the result of the act was death. And then on the basis of the seriousness of the act - and this was determined on the basis of the sentence - it was possible for the judges that if the prosecution qualified an act as murder and the judges thought it was something different, we could say that it wasn't murder, it was something else. But the judges could not, as a result of the fact that they were bound by the factual description, say that a murder was a war crime or they couldn't say that a slight or serious crime was murder. This is something that we would return to the prosecution and we would request that the prosecution make a correct or appropriate request. We couldn't try people for war crimes until people had been accused of such crimes. So these are crimes that couldn't be changed into war crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am going to be more precise. Let's imagine that someone is prosecuted a soldier who allegedly committed the crime of a theft in a house in village X. When you have a look at the documents - and I'll quote on the basis of my memory - if he was pursued according to Rule 150, you would condemn him pursuant to Article 150, and it was with interest that I noted that there were some decisions in which such conduct was punished by two to four months in prison. I won't comment on this, but let's imagine that you interpret Article 142 and you say that this is a theft which could come under Article 142. My question is quite simple: At such a stage, in such a situation, can the judge say that it is Article 142 that is applicable and not Article 150, and thus provide a different qualification of the facts in technical terms? So this is a question of a purely technical nature.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about the amendment of the charges that the court may do. The court must respect the charges. They can't change the charges so that it significantly affects the contents of the charges as specified by the prosecutor. In the documents that we had, the ones that you mentioned, reference would be made to a theft at the time of a war or of an aggravated theft from Croatian or Serbian houses, and then they would keep repeating, theft from Serbian house, Croatian houses, Serbian houses. When you go over to the other side, then they would keep repeating, "theft from a Bosniak house," et cetera. I remember conversations in which we asked, "Why don't you accuse them for something else? These aren't thefts. The army thought they could take anything they wanted as war booty." But this wasn't the opinion that was prevalent. The opinion was that they should prosecute individuals and prove what could be proven. Such indictments were the indictments that would arrive at the court. The court was bound by what the prosecution had said and they could only make changes that went -- that made crimes less serious. But the court couldn't do anything. On the basis of the records, we could see many things but the only possibility was to refer matters back to the prosecution or to judge on the basis of a given indictment. The only possibility we had was to change serious charges into less serious charges but not to do the reverse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday I asked you a question. I asked you about court-martials; I asked you whether such establishments had been established in Zenica. You said no, not as far as you knew. You said you weren't aware of this. Did you know that the Minister of Defence addressed to all the commanders of corps an order requesting that they establish such court-martials? Were you aware of this? And requesting that they be established immediately.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You weren't aware of this. You never knew anything about this?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's possible that I may have heard something like that, but I always had my own opinion of this. Court-martials ad hoc courts [as interpreted], and it would have been logical for me, for the Minister of Defence to say that the corps commander should make preparations so that ad hoc courts could be established immediately. Perhaps they could make documents saying if such-and-such a situation arises, then we will have such-and-such an ad hoc court. But such courts are formed when certain situations arrive, and there must be exceptional circumstances. If this was ordered by the minister, then it is my belief that they could have only drafted a document to prepare for some such thing, and that would be reasonable. In the field, when the situation is very urgent, you should be able to have a document stating that it's necessary to form an ad hoc court. We know the names of the officers. We know who is responsible. And then you would just be able to establish such a court. Not actually form a court; it wouldn't be necessary to issue a decision, an order, et cetera, et cetera. This would have been prepared in advance. If this is what the minister was thinking about, this is quite logical, reasonable, and acceptable. But if the ministers thought that they should just create courts out of nothing, then that is not very understandable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could the witness a document which isn't contested 287. But could you show me the document first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P287. Can you please show -- no, that is not it. 287, I said, and this is 286. And can you please show me the document in B/C/S. Can you please show the document to the witness. Witness, I want to show you a document, and can you please put the English version on the ELMO. This is a document which was signed by Mr. Alagic, and the reference is made to the decree that we have mentioned. And it says here that "The special military courts shall be operating within the 312th Motorised Brigade and the 17th Krajina Mountain Brigade." What can you tell us about this document? As you read this document, what can you tell us about it?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is actually a regular. It serves as a preparatory document for extraordinary and exceptional situations. The order reads: "A special military court should be established in the following brigades." I believe that the order was issued by the corps commander. And the very important thing is that it emphasises the ad hoc and prosecutorial nature of these courts. It says here that "The special military courts shall operate in accordance with the legally effective decree on special military courts. The commanders of the brigades shall be in charge of implementing this order." General Alagic, in my view, was providing for a good organisation of his units by ordering brigade commanders to prepare all the necessary papers that would be used in case a court-martial should start functioning ad hoc. You have to know who the commander of the brigade is. You have to know who will be the officers of the courts. And when the situation arises, you needn't do anything else but pull out the papers and base your decision on those papers. I believe this is good, although things can be done even without that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to address another issue, because I would like to give the Defence and the other Judges time for questions. We have now -- we have seen a document where you are quoted as a member of the commission. You were accompanied by the military police officers. Can you please tell me: What places did you visit with the military police as a judge? I would like you to clarify the situation for me. In answering a question put to you by the Defence, you already clarified some things, but I would like to be absolutely sure that I understand. The military police was made aware of a crime a had been committed. Did they telephone you, a judge, to tell you, "We are going to visit the site. Can you come with us"? Is this what happened in that case?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An on-site investigation in order to secure evidence implied that a judge had to be present. It was the military police that informed the judge to accompany them to the site where he would be able to secure evidence. The police did their job; we, on the other hand, did our job. If something happened and the police had to call the judge - for example, at the detention that they were manning on our behalfs [as interpreted] or something that stemmed from the rights of the detainees, or an on-site inspection - then the police would call the judges. There were also the other situations: When we needed the police to secure a site or to bring somebody in, then the judges would issue orders to the military police, and that was the correlation that we had -- the coordination that we had. I apologise. I apologise. The police was a service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In view of the relationship that you have just described, this relationship was between the military police and the prosecutor and then the prosecutor would inform or would estimate that there were elements for bringing a person before the court or would they ask the judge to conduct an investigation? Is that what happened?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once a judge went to the site, it was the judge's task to record everything and to secure evidence in order to provide for the future admissibility of evidence. All that was collected on the ground, a judge would give to the prosecutor, who would then decide whether he would proceed with the case. A prosecutor would take over everything, and the judge would go back to the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it was the prosecutor who would decide whether to proceed. I'm addressing the issue of Susanj, and the Defence has presented you with a number of documents. I would like to be clear on what happened there. We have seen a number of documents produced by the Defence, and those documents show that you were a member of the commission that was sent, and your name is there. Can you confirm that you were indeed a member of the commission that was sent to investigate the facts concerning the persons who had been killed or murdered or who had died?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a double or dual role there. One role was as judge who was prevented from going to the site of the crime; and my other role was as a member of that commission. The commission was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. I have to interrupt you because we are pressed for time. What was the legal nature of that commission? What was the legal foundation for the establishment of this commission that was in charge of investigating this crime? What was the legal foundation for this commission?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This commission was not in charge of the investigation. General Siber, who was the superior officer to the generals and corps commanders from the area, received information that the judge had been prevented from going there. And then he issued an order for a commission to be established consisting of civilians and soldiers in order to clarify what had happened and what would be done next. As a member of this commission, I stated that I had been prevented from going to the site. I submitted a paper. I requested for the information to be submitted to the superior bodies. So this commission was put in place in order to find out for General Siber who had made a mistake, because the judge had informed him that he was prevented from doing his job properly. And this commission never carried out any further investigation. Now, what the army and the prosecution did after that, I don't know. My duties stopped with the document that I drafted. I only knew -- I only understood that General Siber was concerned with everything being properly documented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your capacity as a judge who acted in this matter, and to the extent the prosecutor was informed, it was up to him to proceed with the case, and your role was -- at one point was stopped.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the obligation of the army and the prosecutor to investigate who was it, who had prevented the judge from performing his duty, and it was up to the prosecutor to investigate whether a crime had indeed been committed on that site. And the judge's duties stopped, there and then, according to the law. It was all in accordance with the law. Please don't be confused by the activity of General Siber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I note here that when you were compiling your report, you indicated who -- you indicated a reference which was 162/93. And I also note that the prosecutor in his documents did not take over this number, 162/93, but he used different numbers, which was 63 or 93 or 94. The number KRI, is it for the prosecutor and does it respond to the same case, or is there a different numeration used by the judges and by the prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The judges used the annotation "KRI" for special actions, and the prosecutor had a different way of marking his documents and their numbers also incorporate letters KT or KTR, so the numbers did not have to correspond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question was: Before you had informed the prosecutor, was he already informed of what had happened? Was he abreast of the situation in your view?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He could have been abreast of the situation, but it would have been a customary procedure for the judge to inform him through an official record, which meant that the prosecutor needed to do something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you have also told us that among the victims, there was a relative of your former colleague, a judge.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He himself could have gone to the prosecutor and reported the incident as a citizen, even before the judge was sent to the site.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You told the prosecutor that there was this relationship, a family relationship that you were aware of.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The prosecutor, like myself, knew Mr. Bozo Markovic, a former judge of the municipal court in Zenica, from before the war. After that he was a defence lawyer, and after that he moved to Croatia and now is a notary public. This man is a member of our profession. The prosecutor knew it; the judges knew that; the defence lawyers knew who he was because he was a well-known name in the town. Like everybody knows Judge Adamovic, everybody knew this particular person whose relative was involved in the case. For example, Mrs. Residovic is not an unknown name in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Everybody is familiar with the name of Maitre Residovic in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please. Microphone for the Presiding Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We resume, and the Judges need another 15 minutes or so. I hope that the Defence is not going to take too much time for their additional questions. Now I give the floor to Judge Swart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Witness, before you came here, I had a lot of questions on criminal procedure in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time you were an investigating judge, notably on public prosecutors, on investigating judges, their relationships, et cetera. But now, after two days, most of these questions have been answered. And also, we got a copy of the Code of Criminal Procedure from the Defence. So I'm very grateful for your having dispelled so many questions, answered so many questions. I still have some questions, and I also want to check with you whether I have understood you properly, because I know that nothing is more easy than to make mistakes in the law of other legal systems than your own. My first question is, in 1993 you were an investigating judge in Zenica. Were you in that capacity for the whole period of 1993 or was it part of the period?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout that entire year, from the moment the court was established to the moment this court stopped existing, I was a judge of that court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And did you remain a investigating judge in the beginning of 1994?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, I was in charge of all the duties. If an investigation was a priority at the moment, then it was my legal obligation to do it. And while I was doing that, I was not assigned to the court duty. However, most often I was in the courtroom acting as the president of a chamber and it was very rarely that I adjudicated cases as an individual judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you the only investigating judge at that period, or were there more persons?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to our internal organisation, every year duties were assigned as to who would be an investigating judge, who would be the president of a chamber, who would deal with appeals. And that's how things were done normally. Having said that, in wartimes, in exceptional circumstances, we did what we could and what we lay our hands on, and my main duty was not to be an investigating judge. I was in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: If I may interrupt you for a moment. My question was simply: Were you the only investigating judge in that period or were there other persons who did the same thing?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There could have been more than one investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you. In a document that was submitted to you this morning by the Defence, a note written by you on the 12th of June, you name yourself a duty judge. Is that something different from an investigating judge, or is this the same kind of thing? The same kind of person, I should say.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is an investigating judge which is on duty out of the regular courtroom hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So basically it is a investigating judge. I wanted to make that sure. Yes.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Now, you talked about Article 156 of the Code of Criminal Procedure that was in force at the time, and this enables you as an investigating judge to take immediate action in urgent situations without a request from the prosecutor and without you having decided on that request. I take it that normally you would use your powers based on that that article pursuant to a request of the local police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to have the text of the law before me in order to avoid confusion. I can see here it, so can I have somebody's assistance with handing it to me. Thank you very much. All the urgent actions can be done by any judge who works in the area, regardless of their territorial competencies, if there is a risk in delay. The police themselves would say that. For example, you go to the site and you can see an iceberg melting and you want to preserve it in evidence. You want to take a photo of that iceberg while it is still there or you want to move it to a cooler place. This is the urgency that I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I understand that perfectly, Witness, that this is the urgency. But I take it that normally the police would phone you and say, "There is an urgent situation and please come to take measures."

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The judge was either at the court or at home. He could only receive information from those whose duty it was to provide information, and the police had such a duty. You know, it's quite possible that something happened in the street nearby but if the judge didn't receive such information from the police, he was not in a position to take any measures of any kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: That is the point of my question. You exclude civilians, and that is what I wanted to know. Yeah. Well, I have a number of questions, and I will shorten them a little bit, on procedures with regard to the death of persons. If a person dies, in all legal systems in the world this has to be officially recorded. And finally, this goes to the civilian authorities, which take a number of measures as the consequence of a death of a person. Now, my questions relate to who is informing the civilian authorities. Let me give an example: A doctor in my own country may draft up a death certificate and send it to the civilian authorities stating the name of the person, the time, the cause of the death, all that. And that would be an official procedure. What would be the case in Bosnia-Herzegovina? What authorities would write these certificates and send them to the civilian authorities? Make it short, please, because of the time.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one can be buried before the person is officially declared to be dead. When someone is brought to a hospital, the doctors write out a certificate. The doctors have to establish that death occurred, and at the same time they fill in a form that shows that perhaps the death was the result of violent action. In such cases, they must inform the police, and the police must take steps to discover whether that is in fact the case or not. In our country, whenever information is received about a body that has been found, the police is immediately called. That is how one proceeds usually. Then the police makes a record, they discuss the matter with the doctor, and this is how one proceeds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So this does not automatically involve an investigating judge or other judge? It depends.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If the doctor says that there are no visible wounds, et cetera, et cetera, well, these are the sort of questions that an investigating judge would also ask, so it's not necessary. But the police is not quite sure about the doctor's opinion or if they themselves observed certain traces, in such cases they might say that the investigating judge should participate in the matter, and the prosecutor on the basis of the record drafted by the investigating judge can take further steps. It might also be possible for the prosecutor to be directly contacted, and he would then turn to the court if traces had been found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I understand that a doctor would distinguish between normal causes of death and abnormal causes of death, and if the abnormal cause seems to have a criminal background, he would send it to the police or to prosecutors or so. What I want to know also in this regard is what was the situation with regard to people who died on the battlefield, because you have no ordinary situation there. Who would ensure that these deaths were properly registered, taken care of?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Doctors who dealt with the case history would deal with this, but in the field only the army - through the military police, the security unit, the medical unit - only they could deal with this and draw certain conclusions and then compile reports and forward the reports. One couldn't expect prosecutors and judges to be in the field when there was ongoing combat. But I'm glad that you saw the records that we made very near the front lines because some commanders in that area, in the area of combat, would calm the situation down so that we could record the cases of death so that families could know that someone died, et cetera, et cetera. This depended on the commanders there. On the whole, we expected to receive information from the army, and it was the army's duty to provide us with such information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in some cases, as we have seen, the dead are not known, so to speak; they have an unknown identity, and then you have a procedure for identifying the dead persons. An example is given by your report on the 12th of June that you have seen this morning, that you had on your table. It starts with an identification of some dead people, and in the presence of witnesses who say who these persons are. Procedures for identifying dead persons do not necessarily imply, I suppose, the presence of an investigating judge; or am I mistaken?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it is related to the procedure, then yes. If it isn't related to the criminal proceedings, then no. I think that is the case everywhere. But the judge must guarantee the identity of the person -- or rather, he will keep a record that a person he has identified has such-and-such characteristics and will confirm that this is the person confirmed. I think on the record it said that a close family member, a relative, was present; that means that the person can be identified, and in such a stage identifying the body just provides the probability that this is in fact the case, this is the identity of the person. And then we continue to deal with this if a trial is initiated. All this is on the basis of reasonable grounds for suspicion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: That already answers many of my questions. I come now to your report of the 12th of June on a number of dead people who have been found in areas of combat operations in the Susanj sector. You remember the report, I suppose? Now, what strikes me is that you go to the hospital in Zenica for the purpose of identification. You identify a number of bodies with the help of family. And the next step in your report is to establish the cause of death of those persons. And it appears that, to summarise what you write, most people have died because of shot wounds. And then at the end, on the last page of your report, you say that it is necessary to take new measures; there must be an investigation in the field. If you want to have this report, it might be given to you. It's DH259, if you'd like to look at it.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's in this binder here. Under 3 or 2?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: It is in your binder, but I don't quite know the number.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it -- no. I've found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So you will see the first pages are concerned with identification. Then you also make a description of the same persons. You establish the cause of death. And then at the last page there are some remarks on what has to be done now. You say, among other things: "An investigation on the spot must be carried out." Later on you say: "An investigating judge should be enabled to go to the area as soon as possible." When you wrote those sentences on the last page, I take it this was a matter of criminal procedure for you, criminal investigation.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I didn't hear the last question because there was a mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: When you wrote on the last pages of your report, of your official note that an investigation on the spot should be carried out and that an investigating judge should go to the area as soon as possible, then I take it you saw the whole matter as a criminal investigation.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I thought that these were the essential actions that should be taken, essential steps that should be taken, and that it shouldn't be delayed, because the bodies that were brought to me, according to what the doctors had said, had been left there and the army left. No one provided information of any kind about anything. And I don't want to burden you with this, but we then searched for information. We tried to find out who had brought them there, from which area, and then we drew certain conclusions as to the area from which they had been brought to us from. Then Mr. Markovic came and said, "It's my relative." He said who the person was. And then when I saw that there were open traces of gunshot wounds, I wanted to check to see whether this really happened in that military zone or whether it had to do with something else. I went to Susanj, and the army prevented me from passing through. I returned, compiled this note, and said, "As soon as possible the judge should be enabled to go to the site. There are a lot of bodies. Don't touch anything. We have to ensure that the procedure is followed because I suspect that a crime has been committed." And that is what has been noted here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I understand you here. But this is not very obvious from the report itself. I thought when I read the report, I said to myself, this could be persons killed during a combat action. There's nothing to indicate in your report itself that there was a different time or place indicating that these were not persons killed during a combat. So you had some extra information, I take it, that is not necessarily included in your report for thinking this was a criminal matter.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: You seemed to nod to me, but could you speak out what you answer it is, in fact, for the record.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think this is contained in the record. There were shots that left traces of gunpowder on the bodies, and this indicates that they were shot at from close range. The first thing that the judge would think about -- the first question a judge would ask is which soldier would shoot as civilians from close range? So then we have reasonable grounds to suspect that a crime has been committed. And as this was the case for a number of individuals, I wanted to check whether this really occurred in a zone of combat action. Then I was told that there was still fighting there, and I said it didn't matter. We have often gone in the field when the fighting was ongoing. I said I wanted to see this for myself. And then my escort and the troops quarrelled and wanted to shoot at each other, and then I returned, drafted this report, this note, and raised the issue. I informed the prosecutor, the military commander, et cetera. That's my duty. And then General Siber reacted -- not at that exact point in time, but a day or two or three later, General Siber asked, "What happened? We've got to form an investigation, ask what's happened, et cetera. It must be possible for the judges to perform their duties."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I may have missed the close range on your report. But on the other hand, I also remark that some of these dead persons have camouflage uniforms and others have hand grenades, so that was the background of my question. Let's now go to another situation in which there also have been written official notes. We have received these documents and I am not quite sure what to think of them. I want them to show to you, because it is a situation somewhat similar in your report. I would like the witness to be shown the documents P332, P333, P334, and P341. Do you have them?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Somebody must show me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: No, they are not in the binder, I must say. I'm sorry. I'll give it to you for the sake of time. I have some copies, if the usher ...

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With regard to your earlier claim about the grenades that they carried and the fact that there was no information about how they were killed, have a look at page 2, where it says that they made a record of "An entry and exit wound in the area of the head and the ribcage. Most of them weren't in uniform." I'm reading this now. This all shows that there were civilians that had been shot and killed from close range. And they even say that one, two, or three of them had parts of military uniforms. In fact, I described the situation as I had found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Now, if you look at these four documents, you will see that they are concerned with a situation that is in some respects similar to the situation in your report, and in other ways dissimilar. There is a covering note saying that a number of bodies have been brought to the Zenica hospital, the same unit where you saw the other bodies. They were brought there to be put through the identification process. That letter doesn't say who brought them. We don't know that from the letter itself. And then there are four annexes, two official notes, a paraffin test, and a photo record. The photo record is not in the possession of the Court, so we don't know what the photos contain. All these letters carry as their head, on top of it the "CSB." And I take it, but just to make sure, I ask you this. This was the civilian police, isn't it, CSB?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Security Services Centre. Yes, CSB, the Security Services Centre. This is the abbreviation. Do you have the judge's record about this? Was a judge called out at all?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: This is one of my questions. If you look at the document -- where is it -- 333, then you see that an official note has been written in the presence of judges and a prosecutor of the Zenica district military court.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One should find this note and get hold of it from the court. This shows that the judge was present. If there is such a note, then the judge was present; if not, then judge wasn't present and someone wrote this off the top of their head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Do you by any chance remember whether you were aware of this yourself or ...?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many bodies were brought to the hospital. We always insisted on being informed. Perhaps I was present. That's a possibility, because on a number of occasions I went to identify bodies, and the conclusion was made and a record of the fact that they had been brought in was made. But I can't remember this. At the moment, it's possible. But as far as the paraffin test is concerned, this is the judge's skill. We asked the paraffin test to be made on the bodies so that we would have sure proof as to whether these people were involved in fighting or not. If they were involved in shooting, then that was something that happened in the conflict; if they weren't involved in shooting and they were still in civilian clothes, then we had reasonable grounds to believe that a crime had been perpetrated or that they had died violently as a result of a combat action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: If you look at the paraffin test - and I resume the results for you, this is 341 - you'll see that the paraffin test is positive for most of the dead persons, and this indicates that they have been using fire weapons. You don't need to check it. I just say this to inform you. There's also the fact that judges of the district military court have been invited to be present at the identification. And this, I take it, suggests a military context; otherwise you would approach the normal criminal court, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any case, they had to address somebody. If the prosecutor of the military prosecutor's office and the judge of the military court were present, then it is to be assumed that the event was related to war operations or had something to do with war activities. When you were talking about the paraffin test being positive, can you please read the remark as well. It says here that "This method is not conclusive." This is just an indicator, because even a simple urination will reveal the same traces. We use this just as the starting point for our subsequent activities. We would hear all the stories, and we would put a mosaic together to see what really happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I realise very well that this is only an indication. But if most of the persons have these traces, then -- and if you see that the judges of the military court are being approached in this matter, then you may think of a military background of the cause of death. My question to you is: If you look at these documents, you see an identification procedure involving a judge and a prosecutor from the military district court, you see another note in which some civilians identify some of the bodies, you see a paraffin test being performed. Is this something -- this is my question, but maybe it's difficult for you to find an answer. But is this a criminal investigation or not? Or can't you be sure?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be sure. I know that something would have been done based on this, within the scope of a further proceedings. This is just identification data and basic indications. The next step that I would take was to verify which units were present in that particular area, whether there were any war operations preceding the event, whether firearms were indeed used. These tests are kept for 24 hours, which means that you may have a prisoner of war after the fighting that was going on for two hours; you can kill him eight hours later and you will end up with the same traces. The judges were very cautious in their proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: May I interrupt you and summarise your position by saying this is not in itself already a criminal investigation but the results of this identification process would justify sending the material to a public prosecutor? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Now, my last question on the matter is the following --

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The last question is the following: If you look again at page -- at the Exhibit P332, the general covering letter, I take it all these documents were sent to the district military court; is that right? Can I read this in the head of the letter?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: It says on the left-hand side: "District military court Zenica." Would these documents automatically arrive at the desk of the public prosecutor there?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They should have, because there is a remark saying that these documents were indeed delivered. But you should verify and check in the court whether the documents indeed were received. Anything can be put on a piece of paper, but you need to check in the court whether the court indeed received these documents on that date. And if this indeed arrived in the court, then according to the normal procedure a judge who received this would send this to the prosecutor, and then prosecutor, once he collected all the documents from the police, from the judge, he would make an evaluation of the whole case. The data saying that bodies had been found does not mean anything on its own. A conclusion had to be drawn from all the available documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Okay. You're now going far beyond my question. I just wanted to verify whether it arrived at the prosecutor's desk, but you derived that from the original, where it says in handwriting "19/1/02"? Is that the reason why you assumed they had been received? What else makes you think they had been received?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no proof that they were received. There is just a police number and an indication that the documents were indeed sent to the court. You have to go to the archives of the court to check whether a document was received bearing that number and that date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Okay. These were my questions. Thank you very much, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Defence, additional questions? We have very little time left.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have a couple of questions for the judge. My first question is relative to your report. Further cross-examination by Ms. Residovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it true, Mr. Adamovic, that the civilian body of authorities, the civilian body whose name is civilian protection and which is part of the civilian authorities, once the combat in the theatre of war is over, they would go to the ground in order to do what we call the clean-up of the ground, or Asanacija, which means that they would collect all the bodies of the soldiers who were killed during the combat? Is it true that once the combat operations were over on the front line the civilian body called civilian protection will go to that ground and carry out the clean-up of that terrain? Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This largely depends on the organisation. The army can do that as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this specific case.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the specific case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this specific case, according to the report, page 4, it says here that "Representatives of the civilian protection collected bodies in the absence of a judge and that's why an on-site investigation could not be done."

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC [Resumed]
